newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Fundamentals favour Sweden over Spain.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Fundamentals favour Sweden over Spain.

text.p: Spanish and Swedish bonds enjoy low inflation, falling interest rates and subdued growth, but analysts said on Friday investors should not become too complacent.
Spanish outperformance may have reached its peak for now, they said, but while Sweden lacks the driving force of European monetary union, its fundamentals suggest it may be a better bet.
"The common theme that unites all these markets, aside from EMU, is the inflation theme," said Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Golman Sachs in London.
"And yesterday in Spain and Sweden we had exceptionally good inflation numbers."

Spanish bond yields scurried to an all-time low on Thursday after data showed year-on year inflation at 3.5 percent in October. The 10-year Bono/Bund spread snapped to a low of 145 basis points, less than half its 330 level in early March.
In Sweden, inflation turned negative for the first time in 37 years with an annualised rate of minus 0.1 percent.
In both countries the news fuelled expectations of further interest rate cuts and boosted bond prices, but analysts said the key differnce for the markets was the EMU factor.

According to forecasts, Sweden stands a better chance of meeting the Masstricht EMU criteria by the planned start date on January 1999 then Spain, but the Swedish crown is not part of Europe's exchange rate grid and the country is undecided on whether it wishes to join a single currency.
Spain, on the other hand, barely misses a chance to reiterate its committemt to EMU, and has concentrated great efforts towards meeting the criteria.
"If the market believes Spain will be in EMU in 1999, then spreads will narrow, but I think that is a bit optimistic," said Ifty Islam, European economist at Merrill Lynch in London.

"The central expectation amongst economists seems to be that Spain will go in a second round." With the risk of external factors -- possibly including a change in market perception that Spain will make EMU in 1999, or an upset to the whole timetable from elsewhere -- disrupting Spain's drive forward on spreads, analysts advised caution.
Instead, both Islam and Bevan advised staying with the long end of Sweden, where economic fundamentals on their own justify spread narrowing.
Bevan set a target for the Swedish/German 10-year yield spread to trade in to 90 or 100 basis points from its currenct 145 level. "Sweden is still a very good story," he said.
But Ken Wattrett, European economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said that without the EMU factor as a pulling force, investors should probably cash in on gains in Sweden.

"You could argue there is scope for rates to come down again, even after the 400 basis points of easing we have had this year," said Wattrett. "But I think we have probably seen the best of the spread tightening in Sweden."
Spanish bonds will continue to outshine Bunds, Wattret said.
"In the short term, sentiment is so positive that there looks to be a bit further to go on the Spanish spread," he said,
"Looking at domestic events, it is hard to come up with anything that will dampen the optimism."

Wattrett said that Thursday's lower-than-expected inflation numbers were enough to justify another 25 basis point cut in interest rates before year end, and said there was also a good chance of another easing in the first quarter of 1997.

But he said some of this had already been discounted. "There is a lot of good news priced into the market already, so from here the magnitude of the spread narrowing will be somewhat less spectacular than it has been in recent weeks."
By year end, Wattrett said the 10-year Bono/Bund spread could well be flirting with the 130 basis point level.
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
